If you ask: what is the meaning of the sending down of the Qur'an on this night? I say: they said it was sent down all at once from the seventh heaven to the lowest heaven, and the noble scribes (*al-Safara al-Kiram*) were commanded to copy it on the Night of Decree, while Jibril (upon him peace) used to bring it down to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) piece by piece.

If you ask: what is the position of these two clauses, ﴿Indeed We have been warners﴾ and ﴿In it every wise matter is decided﴾? I say: they are two resumptive clauses, interwoven [the commentary's note: his phrase "interwoven" is perhaps from *al-laff wa'l-nashr* (folding and unfolding), a rhetorical device established in the science of eloquence, whose explanation follows it]. By them the answer to the oath is explained, which is His words ﴿Indeed We sent it down on a blessed night﴾, as if it were said: "We sent it down, for it is among Our ways to warn and to caution against punishment. The "blessed" (*mubārak*) means abundant in good, because of what Allah makes to be decreed in it of matters in which the benefits of the servants in their religion and their worldly life are contained. Even if nothing were found in it but the sending down of the Qur'an alone, that would suffice as blessing.

The meaning of ﴿yufraq﴾ is: it is distinguished, and every wise matter is decreed and written down, from the provisions of the servants and their terms of life, and all their affairs, from it until the following year. It is also said: the copying of that begins from the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*) on the Night of Acquittal, and the completion occurs on the Night of Decree. The copy of provisions is handed to Mikha'il, the copy of wars to Jibril, and likewise earthquakes, thunderbolts, and landslides, and the copy of deeds to Isma'il, the lord of the lowest heaven, who is a great angel, and the copy of calamities to the Angel of Death. It is reported from some of them: every worker is given the blessings of his deeds, so that praise of him is cast upon the tongues of the creation and awe of him upon their hearts.

It is read *yufarraqu* with the intensive form. And *yufraqu* with its verb in the active voice and *kullu* in the accusative, and the one who distinguishes is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Zayd ibn ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) read *nufarriqu* with the *nūn*. ﴿Every wise matter﴾: every affair that possesses wisdom, that is, it is made to be done as wisdom requires. He made every affair grand and majestic by describing it as wise, then increased its grandeur and gave it magnificence by saying: I mean by this affair an affair originating from Us, issuing from Our presence, in accordance with the requirement of Our knowledge and Our management.

It is permissible that it means the affair which is the opposite of prohibition. Then either it is placed in the position of *furqānan*, which is the verbal noun of "distinguishes," because the meaning of "command" and "distinction" is one, in that when a thing is decided and written, it has been commanded and made obligatory. Or it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to one of the two pronouns in ﴿We sent it down﴾: either the pronoun of the subject, meaning: "We sent it down, commanding a command," or the pronoun of the object, meaning: "We sent it down while it is a command from Us, concerning what must be done."

Then it was said: this Lord is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, whom you acknowledge and confess that He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, if your acknowledgment is from knowledge and certainty. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 44, verses 13–16:

﴿أَنَّىٰ لَهُمُ الذِّكْرَىٰ﴾ means: how will they be mindful and admonished, and how will they keep the promise they made of faith at the lifting of the punishment?

﴿وَقَدْ جَاءَهُمْ رَسُولٌ مُّبِينٌ﴾ [and a clear Messenger had already come to them], something greater and more binding for the obligation of remembrance than the lifting of the smoke. This is what appeared upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of clear signs: the Book, which is itself a miracle, and other miracles. Yet they did not remember, and they turned away from him, and accused him (wa-bahatūhu) [[The phrase "wa-tawallaw 'anhu wa-bahatūhu" means: they accused him of what was not in him. And al-taghwīth is their saying "Wā ghawthāh!" (O, help!), as also in al-Sihah.]] by claiming that ʿAddas, a foreign slave belonging to some of Thaqif, was the one who taught him, and they attributed madness to him.

Then He said: ﴿إِنَّا كَاشِفُو الْعَذَابِ قَلِيلًا إِنَّكُمْ عَائِدُونَ﴾ [Indeed We will lift the punishment a little; indeed you will return], meaning: for the time it takes for Us to lift the punishment from you, you will return to your polytheism, and you will not linger after the lifting in the state you were in of supplication and entreaty.

If you ask: how is ﴿إِنَّا كَاشِفُو الْعَذَابِ قَلِيلًا﴾ consistent according to the view of the one who made the smoke come before the Day of Resurrection? Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 44, verses 17–21:

It is also read ﴿And We certainly tested﴾ with the doubled letter (tashdid), for emphasis, or because the verb governs the people (al-qawm). The meaning of the trial (fitna) is that He gave them respite and widened their provision, and this became the cause of their committing sins and engaging in wrongdoing. Or He tested them by sending Moses to them so that they would believe, but they chose disbelief over faith. Or He stripped them of their kingdom and drowned them. ﴿A noble one﴾ before God and before His believing servants. Or he was noble in himself, because God never sent a prophet except from among the chiefs (sura) and the noblest of his people.

﴿That deliver to me﴾: here anna is explanatory (al-mufassira), because the coming of a messenger to people includes the sense of speech, since he comes to them only as a bringer of good news, a warner, and one who calls to God. Or it is the lightened form (al-mukhaffafa) of the heavy anna, and its meaning is: he came to them with the matter and the message, "deliver to me." ﴿The servants of the Most Merciful﴾ is the object, and they are the Children of Israel. He says: deliver them to me and send them with me, like His saying ﴿So send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them﴾. It is also permissible that it is a call addressed to them: "Deliver to me, O servants of God, what is obligatory upon you toward me: faith in me, acceptance of my call, and following my way." He gives as the reason that ﴿I am a trustworthy messenger﴾, not accused, whom God has entrusted with His revelation and His message.

﴿And do not exalt yourselves against God﴾: this is like the first in both of its aspects. That is, do not be arrogant toward God by treating His messenger and His revelation with contempt. Or: do not be arrogant toward the prophet of God. ﴿With a clear authority﴾, that is, with clear proof, ﴿that you stone me﴾, that is, that you kill me.

It is also read ﴿ʿut﴾ with idgham (assimilation of the two identical letters). Its meaning is that he takes refuge in his Lord and relies on Him to protect him from them and their plotting, so he is unconcerned by their threats of stoning and killing. ﴿So leave me alone﴾: he means that if you do not believe in me, there is no friendship between me and those who do not believe. So step away from me and cut off the means of connection with me, that is, leave me in peace, neither for me nor against me, and do not harass me with your evil and your harm. The reward of one who calls you to what is your success is not this.

﴿That these are a guilty people.﴾ That is: he called upon his Lord with that. It was said: his supplication was, "O Allah, hasten for them what they deserve for their crimes." And it was said: it is his saying, ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people﴾. Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the cause that made them deserve destruction, which is that they were criminals. It was also read: ﴿Inna hā'ulā'i﴾ with a kasra (inna), on the assumption of an implied verb of saying, meaning: so he called upon his Lord and said, "Indeed these are..."

﴿So travel by night with My servants﴾. It was read: ﴿fa-asri﴾ with the hamza cut (from asrā), and with the hamza joined (from sara).

There are two possibilities in it: that a verb of saying is implied after the fa', so that it means "he said: travel by night with My servants"; or that it is the answer to an omitted condition, as if it were said: "He said: if the matter is as you say, then travel by night with My servants," meaning: travel by night with the Children of Israel. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 44, verse 37:

He is Tubba' al-Himyari (Tubba' being the title of the Himyarite kings of Yemen). He was a believer while his people were disbelievers, and for this reason God censured his people but did not censure him. He it was who led armies, made al-Hira (the Hira) a place of confusion [i.e., hayrah, bewilderment], and built Samarqand. It is also said that he destroyed it. Whenever he wrote, he would say: "In the name of God, who possesses land and sea."

The Prophet ﷺ also meant him when he said: "Do not revile Tubba', for he had indeed embraced Islam." [[Narrated by Ahmad, al-Tabarani, al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd, in which there is Ibn Lahi'a from 'Amr ibn Jabir. Both are weak. Habib narrated from Malik from Abu Hazim from Sahl something similar; al-Daraqutni said: Habib alone narrated it, and he is abandoned (matruk). It has a witness from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, narrated by al-Tabarani in his Mu'jam and by Ibn Mardawayh. Muhammad ibn Zakariyya said: from Abu Hudhayfa, from Sufyan.]] And from the Prophet ﷺ: "I do not know whether Tubba' was a prophet or not." [[Narrated by al-Tha'labi through the route of 'Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar from Ibn Abi Dhi'b from al-Maqbari from Abu Hurayrah, with this wording.

What is well known with this chain is: "I do not know whether al-'Ayni is [a prophet] or not, and I do not know whether 'Uzayr is a prophet or not," narrated by Abu Dawud. Likewise al-Hakim, but he said: Dhu al-Qarnayn in place of "'Uzayr." Al-Daraqutni said: 'Abd al-Razzaq alone narrated it, and others narrated it as mursal.]] Prophet." And from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: he was a prophet.

It is also said: he looked at two graves in the region of Himyar and said: "This is the grave of Radwa, and this is the grave of Habba, daughter of Tubba'; neither of them associated anything with God." It is also said: he was the one who clothed the House (the Ka'bah). It was said of the kings of Yemen: al-Tababi'a (the Tubba'ah), because they "follow" (yatba'un); just as it was said: al-Aqyal (the Aqyal), because they "take a midday nap" (yataqayyalun). [[His words "because they take a midday nap": in al-Sihah: taqayyala means to drink at midday; taqayyala fulan abahu means he followed his father.]] The shadow was also called "tab'" because it follows the sun.

If you ask: what is the meaning of His words, "Are they better?" when neither party is better? I say: its meaning is that they are better in strength and power, as in His words, "Are your disbelievers better than those?" after mention of the family of Pharaoh. In the tafsir of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "Are they stronger, or the people of Tubba'?"

Wa-ma baynahuma (and what is between them): that is, between the two kinds (al-jinsayn). ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr recited: wa-ma baynahunna (and what is between them, feminine). And one reading is: mīqātahum (their appointed time) in the accusative, as the subject of inna (indeed), with yawma l-faṣl (the Day of Decision) as its predicate. The meaning: indeed the appointed time for their reckoning and recompense is on the Day of Decision.

Yawma lā yughnī mawlan ʿan mawlan (the day when no protector will avail another protector): any protector whatsoever, whether by kinship or otherwise, shall avail any protector whatsoever in any way, i.e., even a little of benefit. Wa-lā hum yunṣarūn (nor will they be helped): the pronoun refers to the protectors, because in meaning they are plural, since the wording, by its indefiniteness and generality, encompasses every protector. Illā man raḥima llāh (except whom God has shown mercy): this is in the nominative position, as a substitution (badal) for the waw in yunṣarūn; that is, nothing prevents one from punishment except the one whom God has shown mercy. It is permissible that it be in the accusative, as an exception (istithnāʾ).

Innahu huwa l-ʿAzīz (indeed He is the Mighty): none can help against Him one who disobeys Him. Al-Raḥīm (the Merciful): toward whoever obeys Him.

Verily the tree of Zaqqum (al-Zaqqum)... [translation follows below]

Recited: "Inna shajarata al-zaqqum" with the shīn kasrah. There are three dialectal forms: shajara, with the shīn fatḥah or kasrah, and shīra, with a yā'. It is related that when the verse "Is that better as a welcome, or the tree of Zaqqum?" (﴿أَذَلِكَ خَيْرٌ نُزُلًا أَمْ شَجَرَةُ الزَّقُّومِ﴾) was revealed, Ibn al-Zib'ara said: "The people of Yemen call eating butter and dates 'tazaqqum'." So Abu Jahl called for dates and butter and said: "Eat your fill (tazaqqamū), for this is what Muhammad threatens you with." Then it was revealed: ﴿Verily, the tree of Zaqqum is the food of the sinner (al-athīm)﴾, and al-athīm is the grossly wicked one who commits many sins.

It is narrated from Abu al-Darda' that he was teaching a man, and the man kept saying "ṭaʿām al-yatīm" (the food of the orphan). He said: "Say ṭaʿām al-faājir (the food of the wicked one)."

[Maḥmūd (al-Zamakhsharī) said: "It is reported that Abu al-Darda' recited it to a man, and the man did not get the pronunciation of al-athīm right, and kept saying yatīm..." Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munīr) said: there is no proof in this for that. Abu al-Darda's statement is to be understood as clarifying the meaning, so that clarity of meaning helps the learner to recite as it was revealed. This is how al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr interpreted it in his book al-Intiṣār, and it is the correct view, and God knows best.]

O you!

From this it is deduced that replacing one word with another is permissible when it conveys the same meaning. On this basis Abu Hanifa permitted recitation in Persian on one condition: that the reciter conveys the meanings in their completeness without omitting anything from them. They said: this condition shows that it is not a permission at all, because the language of the Arabs, especially the Qur'an which is miraculous in its eloquence, the strangeness of its composition and its styles, contains subtle meanings and aims that no Persian or other tongue can alone bear. Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, did not have good command of Persian, so this was not from him by certainty and insight. ʿAlī ibn al-Jaʿd related from Abū Yūsuf from Abū Ḥanīfa the same as his two companions' rejection of recitation in Persian.

[Kal-muhl (like molten metal) is recited with the mīm both damma'd and fatḥa'd, and it is the dregs (dardī) of oil. [Note: "wa huwa dardī al-zayt" — possibly "rudī al-zayt" as in al-Nasafī's phrasing. (ʿ)]] This is indicated by God's words ﴿on the day when the sky becomes like molten metal﴾ together with His words ﴿and it becomes red like a rose, like oil-dregs﴾. It is also said: it is molten silver and copper. The kāf is in the nominative as a predicate after a predicate, and likewise "yaghlī" (boils). It is recited with the tā' (agreeing with the tree) and with the yā' (agreeing with the food).

Al-ḥamīm is water that is extremely hot, whose boiling has reached its end. It is said to the guards (al-zabāniya): ﴿Seize him and drag him﴾ — that is, drag him harshly and roughly, by seizing him by the collar (talbīb) of the man, and dragging him to prison or to death. From this comes al-ʿutull, which is the coarse and harsh one. It is also recited with the tā' kasrah and ḍammah.

﴿To the middle of the Hellfire﴾: to its midst and its core.

If you say: why was it not said "pour over his head of the ḥamīm," as in God's words ﴿Boiling water is poured over their heads﴾, since the ḥamīm is what is poured and not its punishment? Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 44, verses 51–57:

It is read *fi maqam* (in a station) with a fatḥah, which is the place of standing; the intended meaning is "place," and this is one of the specific terms that has come to be used in the general sense. With a ḍammah (*maqam*), it is the place of residence. *Amin* is derived from your saying: "The man became secure (amina amanatan), so he is *amin*." It is the opposite of *khā'in* (treacherous), and it is applied to the place metaphorically, because a frightening place seems to betray its occupant through the hardships encountered in it.

It is said: *al-sundus* is what is thin of brocade (dībāj), and *al-istabraq* is what is thick of it, and it is an arabicization (ta'rīb) of *istabr*. If you ask: how is it permissible for a non-Arabic word (a'jamī) to occur in the clear Arabic Qur'an? I answer: once it is arabicized, it ceases to be non-Arabic, because the meaning of ta'rīb is that it is made Arabic through handling it, changing it from its original form, and subjecting it to the patterns of i'rāb (grammatical inflection).

*Kadhālika* (thus): the *kāf* is in the nominative, meaning "the matter is thus"; or it is in the accusative, meaning "like that We placed them (in such a state), and We married them (to the ḥūr)."

ʿIkrima read *ḥūrin ʿīn* as an idāfah (construct), meaning "with ḥūr from among the ʿīn." For the ʿayn is either a ḥūr or not a ḥūr, so these are of the ḥūr al-ʿīn, not of the *shuhl* (grey-eyed women) for example. In the reading of ʿAbdullāh: *bi-ʿīsin ʿīn*, and *al-ʿaysāʾ* is the white with a redness over it.

ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read: *lā yudhawqūna fīhā al-mawt* (they do not taste death therein). ʿAbdullāh read: *lā yadhawqūna fīhā ṭaʿm al-mawt* (they do not taste the taste of death therein).

If you ask: how is the first death, which was tasted before entering Paradise, excepted from the death whose tasting is negated therein? I answer: the intention is to say, "They do not taste death at all," so the words *illā al-mawtata al-ūlā* were placed in the position of that, because the past death is impossible to taste in the future. So it is an instance of conditioning on the impossible, as if it were said: If the first death were possible to taste in the future, then they would taste it.

[[Mahmud said: "I have only excepted the first death, which was tasted before entering Paradise, from the death whose tasting is negated therein..." Ahmad said: What he mentioned is based on the view that *al-mawtah* is a substitute (badal), according to the method of the Banu Tamim, who permit substitution from a non-same category. As for the method of the Hijazis, *al-mawtah* is in the accusative as a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ). The essence of the Tamimi dialect: constructing the intended negation in a way that leaves the listener no hope of affirmation, so they say: "There is no one in it except a donkey," meaning: if the donkey is among the two (sets of) people, then there is someone in it; thus they attach the affirmation to something definitely impossible through the negation. On this basis al-Zamakhshari interpreted His saying: "Say: none in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah," meaning: if Allah is among those in the heavens and earth, then among the heavens and earth there is one who knows the unseen. So when the listener recoils from the affirmation of the first, the recoil extends to the affirmation of the second, and he is definitively negated. And Allah knows best.]].

*Wa-quriʾa wa-waqāhum* with tashdīd (intensive form). *Faḍlan min rabbika*: a gift (ʿaṭāʾ) from your Lord and a reward (thawāb), meaning: all that He gave the pious of the bliss of Paradise and deliverance from the Fire. It is also read *fadlun*, meaning: that is a bounty.
